sorting/01_insertion_sort: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix one element at a time: take the next value, shift every larger element of the prefix one slot to the right, and drop the value into the gap. It is the sort you reach for on tiny or nearly sorted input, and it is stable because equal values never shift past each other. The common slip is stopping the scan before index 0, so the first element can never move. Quadratic time in general, linear when the input is almost sorted, no extra space.
sorting/02_merge_sort: Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively, and merges the two sorted runs by repeatedly taking the smaller head. It is the comparison sort to name when you need a guaranteed bound or stability, and the merge step on its own is a tool for combining sorted lists. Taking the left run on ties is what keeps it stable, and forgetting to append the leftover run after one side empties loses elements. Always O(n log n) time, O(n) extra space for the merged runs.
sorting/03_quick_sort: Quick sort picks a pivot, partitions the range so everything at most the pivot sits to its left, swaps the pivot into that final slot, and recurses on both sides. Lomuto partition keeps a small region at the front and grows it by one swap whenever the scan meets a value at most the pivot. The pivot must stay out of the scan and out of both recursive calls; that is where off-by-one bugs live. O(n log n) on average, quadratic on sorted input, in place, not stable.
sorting/04_heap_sort: Heap sort first turns the array into a max-heap in place by sifting down from the last parent to the root, then repeatedly swaps the root, the maximum, with the last slot of the heap region and shrinks that region by one. The sorted suffix grows from the right while the heap shrinks from the left. The usual mistake is sifting over the whole array instead of only the shrunk heap, which drags sorted values back in. Always O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space, not stable.
sorting/05_counting_and_bucket_sort: Counting sort and bucket sort skip comparisons entirely. Counting sort indexes an array of counts by value and walks the counts in order, which suits small non-negative integers. Bucket sort drops floats in [0, 1) into n buckets by int(x * n), so bucket order is value order, then sorts each bucket and concatenates. People size the counts array as max instead of max plus one, or assume a bucket is already sorted. Counting is O(n + k) for max value k; bucket is O(n) on average.
sorting/06_python_sort_keys_and_stabilit: Python's sorted takes a key function and is stable, and those two facts cover most sort-by-several-fields questions. To sort by department ascending then salary descending, use the tuple key (dept, -salary); negating a numeric field flips just that field. The two-pass alternative sorts by the minor key first and then by the major key, relying on stability to keep the minor order inside each group. The classic error is doing the passes in the wrong order or sorting the original list instead of the first output. O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
searches/01_binary_search_variants: Binary search on a sorted array halves the range each step. The plain version uses a closed range and stops when it is empty; lower bound finds the first index with a value at least x, upper bound the first index with a value greater than x, both over a half-open range that may return the length. The count of x is upper minus lower. What people mix up is the comparison: lower bound moves lo past values strictly smaller than x, upper bound also past equal values. O(log n) time, O(1) space.
searches/02_binary_search_on_answer: Binary search on the answer solves smallest-value-that-works problems: when a yes/no check is monotone, so that once a value works every larger one works too, you binary search the value instead of an array. For shipping packages, can_ship greedily fills ships and the search runs over capacities from the heaviest package to the total weight. The usual mistake is a low bound below the max weight, or moving hi to mid minus one when mid itself might be the answer. Time is the check cost times the log of the range, O(n log S).
searches/03_bfs_grid_shortest_path: BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted grid because it explores in layers: every cell in the queue at distance d is handled before any cell at d + 1, so the first time the target leaves the queue its distance is final. Use a deque so popleft is constant time, and store each cell's distance when it is enqueued. The bug that bites is marking visited on pop instead of on enqueue, which lets cells enter the queue many times. O(rows times cols) time and space.
searches/04_dfs_recursive_and_iterative: DFS visits everything reachable from a start node by going as deep as possible before backing up. The recursive version is the definition: mark, record, recurse into unvisited neighbours. The iterative version uses an explicit stack, and to reproduce the same order it must push neighbours in reverse so the first neighbour is on top, and mark a node when popped, skipping stale copies. Marking on push instead is the classic bug that changes the order. O(V + E) time, O(V) space for the visited set and stack.
searches/05_connected_components: Counting connected components in an undirected graph means counting how many times you have to start a fresh search. Build the adjacency list with each edge stored in both directions, then loop over every node and run a BFS from any node not yet seen, bumping the count once per start. Every search marks exactly one whole component, and an isolated node is a component on its own. People forget the reverse direction of each edge, or forget to loop over all nodes so isolated nodes go uncounted. O(V + E) time and space.
searches/06_multi_source_bfs_01_matrix: Multi-source BFS answers distance-to-the-nearest-zero for every cell in one pass. Put every zero into the queue at the start with distance 0, mark every other cell as unreached, and run an ordinary layer-by-layer BFS; the layer in which a cell is first reached is its distance to the closest source, because all sources expand at the same speed. The mistake is running a separate BFS per cell, which is quadratic, or forgetting to seed all sources before the loop begins. O(rows times cols) time and space.
graphs/01_adjacency_list_bfs_dfs: An adjacency list is a list of lists where adj[u] holds the neighbours of u, and it is the starting point for almost every graph problem. BFS uses a deque and marks a node when enqueued so each node enters the queue once; DFS uses a stack, pushes neighbours in reverse so the smallest pops first, and marks a node when popped so stale copies are skipped. The thing people forget is storing an undirected edge in both directions. Building the list and either traversal is O(V + E) time, O(V) extra space.
graphs/02_topological_sort_kahn_and_dfs: Topological sort orders the nodes of a directed acyclic graph so every edge points forward, which is how you schedule tasks with prerequisites. Kahn's version counts indegrees, starts a queue with every node of indegree 0, and each time a node is removed decrements its neighbours, enqueuing any that drop to 0. The DFS version reverses the post-order and spots a cycle when it meets a node still on the current path. People forget to compare the output length with n: fewer means a cycle. O(V + E) time and space.
graphs/03_union_find: Union-find keeps n elements in disjoint sets and answers two questions fast: which set does x belong to, and are a and b in the same set. parent[x] points toward the root of its set, and a root points to itself. Find follows parents to the root and compresses the path so later lookups are nearly free; union hangs the smaller tree under the bigger root. People skip path compression, or compare raw elements instead of their roots, which breaks the connected check. Near constant time per operation, O(n) space.
graphs/04_kruskal_mst: Kruskal builds a minimum spanning tree by sorting the edges by weight and scanning from cheapest to most expensive, keeping an edge only when its two endpoints are not yet connected. Union-find answers that connected question in near-constant time, and every rejected edge is one that would close a cycle. A disconnected graph gives a forest instead of a tree. People forget to sort first or forget to stop after n minus 1 accepted edges. Sorting dominates at O(m log m) time, with O(n) space for the parent array.
graphs/05_prim_mst: Prim grows a minimum spanning tree from one start node: a heap holds the edges leaving the tree, you pop the cheapest, skip it if its far end is already inside, otherwise add the node and push its edges to outside nodes. The invariant is that the heap always holds every edge crossing from the tree to the rest, so the cheapest pop is always safe. The stale-entry check is what people miss: a node can be pushed several times and only the first pop counts. O(m log m) time, O(m) space for the heap.
graphs/06_dijkstra: Dijkstra finds shortest distances from a source in a graph with non-negative edge weights. A heap holds (distance, node) pairs; popping the smallest gives a node whose distance is now final, and you relax each out-edge by pushing a better distance for the neighbour whenever one appears. Because old entries stay in the heap, you must skip any popped pair whose distance is larger than the recorded best. People forget that skip, or run it on negative weights where final-when-popped fails. O(m log m) time, O(n + m) space.
trees/01_traversals_recursive_and_iterat: Preorder, inorder and postorder are the three ways to visit a binary tree, and they differ only in where the visit sits relative to the two recursive child calls: before, between or after. Inorder on a binary search tree gives sorted values. Iterative preorder uses a stack and pushes the right child before the left so the left pops first; iterative inorder walks left pushing every node, pops and visits, then moves right. Pushing children in the wrong order is the usual slip. O(n) time, O(h) stack space for height h.
trees/02_bfs_level_order_and_height: Level order traversal lists the values of a binary tree one level at a time using a queue. The trick is to drain exactly the nodes in the queue when the level starts, a loop of range(len(queue)); their children go in for the next round. Height in levels then falls out as the number of rounds, with an empty tree at 0 and a single node at 1. People re-read the queue length inside the loop instead of fixing it once up front, which mixes levels together. O(n) time, O(w) space for the widest level.
trees/03_bst_insert_search_delete: A binary search tree keeps every value in the left subtree smaller than the node and every value in the right subtree larger, so search, insert and delete each walk one root-to-leaf path and an inorder walk reads the values back sorted. Insert attaches a new leaf where the walk falls off. Delete splices out a node with at most one child; for two children it copies the inorder successor, the leftmost node of the right subtree, then deletes that successor from the right subtree. Deleting the original value instead of the successor's is the classic bug. O(h) per operation.
trees/04_balanced_and_depth: The depth of a binary tree is one more than the depth of its taller child, computed bottom up, with an empty tree at 0. A tree is height-balanced when at every node the two subtree heights differ by at most 1. The one-pass check reuses the height walk: it returns the height for a balanced subtree and -1 the moment any subtree fails, passing that -1 straight up. The mistake is calling a separate height function at every node, which costs far more, or treating a difference of exactly 1 as unbalanced. O(n) time, O(h) space.
trees/06_serialize_and_deserialize: Serializing a binary tree writes it as a string and deserializing rebuilds the same tree. Preorder with an explicit marker like # for every missing child is unambiguous, so encoding emits the value, then the left subtree, then the right, and decoding consumes tokens from one shared deque in the same order: take a token, build the node, then its left subtree, then its right. People forget the separator, which merges 12 and -3 into 1, 2, 3, or skip the None markers, which loses the shape. O(n) time, O(n) space.
linked_lists/01_build_print_insert_delet: The basic linked list operations are building from a Python list with a moving tail, walking to print the values, inserting at an index, and deleting the first node holding a value. A dummy node in front of the head is the whole trick: with it, inserting at index 0 and deleting the head become ordinary cases, and you always return dummy.next. People lose the head by skipping the dummy, or walk one step too far so prev is not the node before the slot. Build and delete are O(n), insert is O(index), O(1) extra space.
linked_lists/02_reverse_iterative_and_re: Reversing a singly linked list flips every next pointer so the old tail becomes the head. The iterative version walks three pointers: save cur's next before you cut, point cur back at prev, then advance both; when cur falls off the end, prev is the new head. The recursive version reverses the rest first, then hangs the current node behind its old next node and sets its own next to None. Cutting before saving the rest is the classic bug that loses the tail. O(n) time; O(1) space iterative, O(n) stack recursive.
linked_lists/03_middle_with_fast_and_slo: The fast and slow pointer pair finds the middle of a linked list in one pass without counting: slow steps one node, fast steps two, and when fast can no longer take two more steps slow is in the middle. For an even length there are two middles, and the condition while fast and fast.next leaves slow on the second one; checking fast.next and fast.next.next instead picks the first. The common slip is testing only fast, which crashes on fast.next.next at the end. O(n) time, O(1) space.
linked_lists/04_detect_cycle_floyd: Floyd's tortoise and hare detects a cycle in a linked list in constant space: slow steps one, fast steps two, and inside a cycle fast must eventually land on slow, while without a cycle fast runs off the end. To find where the cycle starts, keep one pointer at the meeting node, restart the other at the head, and step both by one; they meet exactly at the entry. People compare node values instead of node identity with is, or restart both pointers instead of one. O(n) time, O(1) space.
linked_lists/07_reverse_nodes_in_k_group: Reverse nodes in k-group reverses each run of k consecutive nodes and leaves a final shorter run untouched, changing links rather than values. Per group, probe k nodes ahead from the node before the group and stop if the list ends; then run the usual three-pointer reverse over just that group with prev seeded to the node after the group, so the old head links into the next group; finally hook the node before the group to the k-th node and advance to the old head, now the tail. Forgetting that seed leaves the group dangling. O(n) time, O(1) space.
stacks/01_array_stack_and_queue_via_two_: A stack on a Python list uses the end as the top, so push is append and pop and peek work on the last element. A queue built from two stacks pushes new items onto an inbox and serves dequeue and peek from an outbox, refilling the outbox by draining the inbox only when the outbox is empty; the drain reverses the items into queue order. Refilling while the outbox still has items breaks that order and is the one bug to avoid. Every element crosses once, so n operations cost O(n) total, O(n) space.
stacks/05_asteroid_collision: Asteroid collision keeps a stack of survivors and walks the asteroids left to right. Right-movers always push. A left-mover fights the stack top while that top is a right-mover: a smaller top explodes and the fight continues, an equal top kills both, a bigger top kills the newcomer. Asteroids moving the same way, or a left-mover meeting a left-moving top, never collide and simply push. People forget to keep fighting after popping a smaller top, or compare signed values instead of sizes. O(n) time and space; each asteroid is pushed and popped at most once.
monotonic_stacks/01_next_greater_element: Next greater element finds, for each value, the first value to its right that is strictly bigger. The stack holds indices still waiting for an answer, with values decreasing from bottom to top; each new element pops every waiting index whose value it beats and becomes their answer, then joins the stack. Anything left at the end stays at -1. The comparison must be strict, and people often store values instead of indices and then cannot write the answer back. O(n) time, each index pushed and popped once, O(n) space.
monotonic_stacks/02_previous_smaller_ele: Previous smaller element finds, for each value, the nearest value to its left that is strictly smaller. Walking left to right, the stack holds values strictly increasing from bottom to top; pop everything greater than or equal to the current value, and whatever survives on top is the answer, then push the current value. A popped value can never be anyone's answer later because the current value is smaller and closer. The slip is a strict comparison on the pop, which wrongly treats equal values as smaller. O(n) time, O(n) space.
monotonic_stacks/03_online_stock_span: Online stock span answers, one price per day, how many consecutive days ending today had a price at most today's. The stack keeps (price, span) pairs with prices strictly decreasing from bottom to top; for a new price, pop every top with price at most today's and add its span to today's, since that day already covered its own run, then push today's pair. People try to recount days from scratch, which is quadratic, or forget to absorb the popped spans. Amortized O(1) per day, O(n) space worst case.
monotonic_stacks/04_sum_of_subarray_mini: Sum of subarray minimums adds up the minimum of every contiguous subarray. Count contributions instead of subarrays: element i is the minimum of (i minus left) times (right minus i) subarrays, where left is the previous strictly smaller index and right the next smaller-or-equal index. One increasing stack of indices finds both at the moment it pops i, and a sentinel pass at the end pops everything left. Using the same strictness on both sides double counts subarrays with repeated minima, and people forget the modulo. O(n) time, O(n) space.
monotonic_stacks/05_remove_k_digits: Remove k digits deletes k characters from a decimal string to leave the smallest number. Greedy with a stack: a bigger digit standing in front of a smaller one should go first, so while deletions remain pop any top larger than the incoming digit, then push it; the kept digits stay non-decreasing. If deletions are left over the stack is sorted, so cut from the end. Finally strip leading zeros and return 0 for an empty result. People forget the leftover cut or the empty-string case. O(n) time, O(n) space.
